claims.text: CodePipeline's default execution mode is `SUPERSEDED`.
CodePipeline's `SUPERSEDED` execution mode locks a stage to one execution at a time.
CodePipeline's `SUPERSEDED` execution mode only protects an execution once it is actually running.
In CodePipeline with `SUPERSEDED` execution mode, a newer execution can overtake one that is still waiting to enter a locked stage, dropping it before it ever starts.

If a CodeBuild stage in a CodePipeline pipeline runs `pulumi up` and enough commits land while it's busy, a queued execution waiting behind it can be superseded and never run at all, silently skipping a deployment rather than colliding with one already in progress.

Setting a CodePipeline pipeline's execution mode to `QUEUED` causes waiting executions to form a queue so each one runs in turn rather than a later commit erasing an earlier one that never got its turn.
CodePipeline's `QUEUED` execution mode requires a V2 pipeline.
To use `QUEUED` execution mode, you must set both `executionMode` and `pipelineType` when defining the pipeline.
The AWS CLI's `create-pipeline` command can be used to set the `executionMode` and `pipelineType` when defining a CodePipeline pipeline.
The AWS CLI's `update-pipeline` command can be used to set the `executionMode` and `pipelineType` when defining a CodePipeline pipeline.
The `aws.codepipeline.Pipeline` resource has an `executionMode` input.
The `aws.codepipeline.Pipeline` resource has a `pipelineType` input.
Configuring a CodeBuild project (or CodePipeline source stage) to trigger on git tag events rather than branch pushes makes promotion a single, traceable Git operation.
Configuring a CodeBuild project (or CodePipeline source stage) to trigger on git tag events rather than branch pushes ensures production never deploys from an untested commit.
CodeBuild projects, CodePipeline pipelines, IAM roles, and Parameter Store entries are themselves AWS resources.
CodeBuild projects, CodePipeline pipelines, IAM roles, and Parameter Store entries can be defined with Pulumi using the AWS provider.
Using Pulumi ESC to broker short-lived cloud credentials avoids storing provider keys as pipeline variables at all.
When two runs reach the same Pulumi Cloud stack at once, Pulumi Cloud grants the deployment lease to only one of them.
When two runs reach the same Pulumi Cloud stack at once, the run that does not get the lease fails its `pulumi up` with an update conflict.
Azure Pipelines can prevent concurrent-run update conflicts at the source with an exclusive lock check on the environment a deployment job targets.
An Azure Pipelines exclusive lock check is added from an environment's 'Approvals and checks' tab.
Azure Pipelines supports setting a `lockBehavior` property on the stage that references an environment's exclusive lock check.

In Azure Pipelines YAML, a stage can set `lockBehavior: sequential` alongside a deployment job that runs the `Pulumi@1` task with `command: up`, targeting stack `acme/website/production` with `args: --yes`.
Azure Pipelines' default `lockBehavior` value is `runLatest`.
With Azure Pipelines `lockBehavior: runLatest`, only the most recently queued run ever acquires the lock.
With Azure Pipelines `lockBehavior: runLatest`, an older run stuck waiting behind the most recently queued run is passed over rather than eventually applied.
Azure Pipelines `lockBehavior: runLatest` is acceptable for a preview environment where only the newest state matters.
Azure Pipelines `lockBehavior: runLatest` is not acceptable for a stack where every update needs to land.
With Azure Pipelines `lockBehavior: sequential`, every queued stage runs against the lock in order, one at a time.
Azure Pipelines `lockBehavior: sequential` runs queued stages in the same way that Pulumi Cloud itself serializes updates to a stack.
The Azure DevOps provider's `azuredevops.CheckExclusiveLock` resource can be used to manage an Azure Pipelines exclusive lock check as code.
Azure DevOps itself—including projects, repositories, pipelines, and service connections—can be managed as code with the Azure DevOps provider in the Pulumi Registry.
Pulumi offers native version control integrations for popular Git hosts, independent of TeamCity.
With a Pulumi version control integration configured, Pulumi Cloud posts infrastructure-change summaries as pull request comments.
With a Pulumi version control integration configured, Pulumi Cloud posts status checks for infrastructure changes.
With a Pulumi version control integration configured, Pulumi Cloud links each stack update back to the commit and pull request that produced it.
When two runs of the same TeamCity build configuration reach the same Pulumi stack at once, Pulumi Cloud grants the update lease to only one of them.
When Pulumi Cloud grants the stack update lease to only one of two concurrent runs, the other run's `pulumi up` fails with an update conflict.
TeamCity's own default behavior is to let build configurations run concurrently against as many free agents as it has available.
TeamCity build configurations have an advanced option called 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' located under that configuration's General Settings.
TeamCity's 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' option defaults to 0, meaning unlimited concurrent builds.
Setting TeamCity's 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' option to 1 causes a second build that would otherwise start immediately to be queued behind the first build instead.
When TeamCity's 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' option is set to 1, a queued second build runs only once the first build finishes.
A clean TeamCity build agent starts with an empty plugin cache.
Because a clean build agent starts with an empty plugin cache, Pulumi re-downloads its provider plugins on every run in that scenario.
In Azure Pipelines, adding an exclusive lock check to the environment a deployment job targets with `lockBehavior: sequential` on the stage serializes deployments so they do not run concurrently.
Azure Pipelines supports an exclusive lock check that can be added to the environment a deployment job targets.
Azure Pipelines supports a `lockBehavior: sequential` setting on a stage.

There exists a Pulumi documentation page at /docs/iac/operations/continuous-delivery/azure-devops/#serialize-deployments-with-an-exclusive-lock describing how to serialize deployments with an exclusive lock.
AWS CodePipeline has a pipeline configuration option called "execution mode" that can be set to `QUEUED`.
Setting AWS CodePipeline's execution mode to `QUEUED` causes waiting executions to run in turn (serially).
AWS CodePipeline's default execution mode allows a newer pipeline execution to supersede an older execution that is still waiting to start.
There exists a Pulumi documentation page at /docs/iac/operations/continuous-delivery/aws-code-services/#serialize-pipeline-executions describing how to serialize AWS CodePipeline executions.
TeamCity has a build configuration setting called "Limit the number of simultaneously running builds" that can be set to `1`.
Setting TeamCity's "Limit the number of simultaneously running builds" to `1` on a build configuration prevents concurrent builds for that configuration.
There exists a Pulumi documentation page at /docs/iac/operations/continuous-delivery/teamcity/#limit-concurrent-builds describing how to limit concurrent TeamCity builds.
